sources.news_title: Breanna Stewart Says WNBA Inclusivity Is A 'Big Thing' After Sophie Cunningham Trans Comment
sources.text:
New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart has broken her silence over the WNBA controversy sparked by Indiana Fever’s Sophie Cunningham‘s comments about trans athletes in women’s sports. The league has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women should be allowed to participate in sports.
Breanna Stewart Is All For ‘Safe Space’
In an interview with the New York Post, Stewart addressed Cunningham’s comments. It seemed like both women have different opinions regarding the matter.
“Everyone is entitled to their own opinion,” Stewart said. “This league is incredibly inclusive, in what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So we don’t want to take that platform away.”
Stewart continued, “We just want to make sure that everyone is still educated and knows that the things that brought this league together – between the fight and the grit and the camaraderie – we can’t let that take us apart by outside hate.”
She Believes In Not Turning Anyone ‘Away’ As It’s ‘Not Right’
Stewart emphasized that the “inclusivity” is the “big thing” for her.
“I don’t want to turn anyone away at the door because that’s not right either. But I know for a fact that people have a safe space here when they come to these games, and that’s something that… is really precious, and you have to hold on to and make sure that doesn’t change,” she explained.
Stewart also mentioned the competing rallies over the issue outside the Liberty vs. Fever game, highlighting WNBA’s platform to stir discussion rather than to ignite hate.
“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has, and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” she said.
- Breanna Stewart is one of the most accomplished basketball players in history, and she co-founded Unrivaled, the innovative 3-on-3 women’s basketball league with Napheesa Collier.
- In 2023, they started the winter league, which consisted of 30 of the top women’s players competing in three-on-three and one-on-one games.
- Earlier this year, Unrivaled had a sold-out night, which became a defining moment in women’s basketball.
- Stewart and Collier’s Unrivaled joined forces with TOGETHXR, co-founded by world champion athletes Sue Bird, Alex Morgan, Chloe Kim, Simone Manuel, and sports media veteran Jessica Robertson.
- In January 2026, the Innovators of the Year award was presented to Collier and Stewart.
- Stewart is so popular that she gets birthday wishes from fans, and she responds.
Sophie Cunningham Stands By What She Said
In an ESPN article published in July, Cunningham said she wants “protect young girls in the locker room,” where “they shouldn’t have to go against biological men.” This ignited a firestorm that put the WNBA on center stage of a contentious political debate.
“I said what I said. I think it’s kind of common sense,” Cunningham said says later. “And I think I’ll always believe in that. I think it’s really important to protect children, and that’s little girls who are also involved in that category. I stand on what I said.”
However, despite her comments regarding keeping trans athletes out of the WNBA, Cunningham claims that her political views are “very much in the middle.”
“I’m very much in the middle,” she said. “I agree with things on both sides, disagree with things on both sides. And that’s all I’ve ever said about my political beliefs. But people love to assume.”
WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert Speaks Up About The Issue
Cathy Engelbert, WNBA’s commissioner, spoke up about the trans athlete issue. As reported by The Guardian, she denounced people who are trying to “sow divisiveness” as the league grapples with a debate over transgender athletes.
Engelbert made the comments on Thursday before the Indiana Fever’s loss to the Dallas Wings at the American Airlines Center in the Victory Park neighborhood of downtown Dallas. Demonstrators showed up outside, as they have at other venues since Cunningham’s stance on barring transgender girls and women from girls’ and women’s sports.
“People are trying to use the league to sow divisiveness,” Engelbert said. “We’re being the center of political football for people who have never watched the WNBA, never have written about the WNBA or reported on the WNBA.”
Her statement echoed NBA commissioner Adam Silver’s recent use of “political football” to describe the debate that has engulfed the WNBA.
As per the collective bargaining agreement of the league, “only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA.” However, it does not include any more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth. Earlier this month, Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, who are former NBA players, declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women. A memo was sent by Engelbert this month to team presidents and general managers saying the league would accepting transgender women in women’s basketball.
“There’s always going to be haters out there and we denounce it,” she stated. “But that’s what happens when you have made it as a legitimate sports media and entertainment product.”

sources.news_title: Breanna Stewart wants safe space as transgender debate sparks rallies at Fever games
sources.text:
Indiana Fever forward Makayla Timpson (21) defends New York Liberty forward Breanna Stewart (30) in the first half of a game on Aug. 11 in Indianapolis. Stewart is a Cicero-North Syracuse graduate.
NEW YORK (AP) — New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart, a Cicero-North Syracuse graduate, has always seen the WNBA as an inclusive place that has served as a safe space for both its fans and the players. That’s been challenged lately.
The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA. Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
There have been small rallies and protests outside Indiana Fever games after the issue came to a head when Sophie Cunningham of the Fever said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. There were a pair of peaceful rallies representing both sides of the transgender issue that took place before the Fever faced the New York Liberty on Saturday night. The Liberty won the game 109-102.
“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” Stewart told a small group of reporters Saturday morning. “I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space.”
Cunningham felt that all the attention that her comments have garnered has been positive by bringing more fans to the game.
“You have a lot of new fans, not only just watching, but coming to games and seeing the environment and seeing the talent,” she said before the game. “I think anytime you can get more eyes on the W, that’s an awesome thing, because then that inspires other young kids that maybe have never seen the game or heard about the game or been to a game, they get that experience. So I definitely think that it’s been a very positive thing.”
At least three fans were asked by WNBA security personnel to cover shirts that had messages about transgender women participating in women’s sports during last Sunday’s game at Atlanta between the Dream and the Fever. The league later said the fans should have been free to wear those shirts.
Stewart said Liberty fans specifically, but WNBA fans in general, come to games because “they can feel like they can be themselves in whatever capacity that is and we don’t want to lose sight of that."
The Liberty forward said everyone is entitled to their own opinion and if that stops being allowed there are much bigger issues. However, she said, trying to divide teams and players shouldn't be tolerated.
“If we don’t allow (free speech), we need to like really kind of go back and look at more things. I think the bigger thing is people are trying to divide us as teams, but also as teammates or as opponents," she said. "This league is incredibly inclusive and what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So, we don’t want to take that platform away.”
Stewart has been an ally for the transgender community during her career. She faced some online backlash last year when one of her signature shoes had a Harry Potter theme to it. Stewart is a huge fan of the Harry Potter books and subsequent movies by author J.K. Rowlings, who has drawn criticism for her anti-trans stance.
Stewart has donated royalties from that shoe to The Trevor Project, a suicide prevention and crisis intervention nonprofit organization for LGBTQ+ youth.

sources.news_title: Liberty’s Breanna Stewart bullish on ‘superpower’ WNBA must protect as trans athlete debate sparks rallies
sources.text:
Breanna Stewart wanted to wait.
After Friday’s practice, with Saturday’s Liberty-Fever showdown already carrying the usual weight of a marquee WNBA game, Stewart was asked about the competing rallies planned outside Barclays Center ahead of tip-off.
		
		
		
				
			We’ve got you covered on the Liberty beat

tRY IT NOW
“I honestly would love to weigh in tomorrow,” Stewart said.
Saturday morning, she did.
Less than 24 hours later, Stewart gathered with a small group of reporters, including The Post, for an in-depth conversation about the scheduled demonstrations, the WNBA’s approach to transgender inclusion and what she believes the league should protect as its audience continues to grow.
Her central message was less about choosing a side than refusing to let the debate fracture what she views as one of the league’s defining qualities, which is its ability to make people feel they belong.
“The inclusivity [of the league] is the big thing for me,” said Stewart before scoring a team-high 22 points in the Liberty’s 109-102 win over the Fever. “I don’t want to turn anyone away at the door because that’s not right either. But I know for a fact that people have safe space here when they come to these games, and that’s something that … is really precious, and you have to hold on to and make sure that doesn’t change.”
Fever star Sophie Cunningham’s comment in an ESPN article published last month, in which she said she wants “to protect … young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” ignited a firestorm that put the WNBA on center stage of a contentious political debate.
In the subsequent weeks, rallies in support of Cunningham and “protect girls in sport” have been scheduled outside Fever games, including in Seattle, Dallas and Chicago. Counterprotests supporting transgender inclusion have also been planned.
Outside Barclays Center on Saturday was expected to be the next host site of both demonstrations.
“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has,” Stewart said, “and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have.”
Earlier this month, former NBA players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White announced they were planning to enter the 2027 WNBA draft because the WNBA’s stance on transgender athletes’ participation remains unclear.
The WNBA created an anti-hate task force to address multiple issues facing the league, but it hasn’t established a definitive policy addressing transgender athlete eligibility.
The league issued a statement last week, saying, in part, “There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA, and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others.”
Stewart said the absence of that policy, though, has left room for controversy to fester.
“Of course, if the league kind of had the rules set in place on inclusivity, it would kind of make it a cleaner picture for everyone else,” Stewart said. “With that, I’m definitely deferring to the WNBA and the task force. … Hopefully they were thinking about this beforehand … [and] didn’t come up just now.”
There should be a distinction between league policy and individual belief.
The WNBA has long been far more outspoken compared to other major American professional sports leagues on issues of social justice and equality.
“That’s our superpower,” Stewart said. “The ability to kind of come together.”
Stewart believes that willingness to use its collective voice remains a strength, even as the league attracts new fans who may not share the same politics.
“Everyone is entitled to their own opinion,” Stewart said. “This league is incredibly inclusive, in what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So we don’t want to take that platform away. We just want to make sure that everyone is still educated and knowing that the things that brought this league together between the fight and the grit and like the camaraderie, we can’t let that take us apart by outside hate.”
Stewart, who identifies as an ally of the transgender community, doesn’t have all the answers, and she didn’t offer a clear-cut resolution to a divisive issue. She expressed her desire for the league to preserve room for disagreement without allowing disagreement to become division.
“There’s so many different ways to be,” she said. “And you see there’s so many different personalities and people in our league, and who they love and what they stand for, and all these different types of things. And that doesn’t have to mean that we have to pick one.”
For Stewart, that point is worth protecting as the WNBA enters a new era of visibility.

sources.news_title: 'Stunts for attention': WNBA star Breanna Stewart wants 'a safe space' amid anti-trans rallies
sources.text:
Ever since Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham spoke out against transgender women in women’s sports, the league has dealt with anti-trans rallies outside of Indiana Fever games as fans express their support for Cunningham and her views. Now, one WNBA star wants a “safe space.”
As discourse about transgender athletes has engulfed the league, two-time WNBA MVP Breanna Stewart has made it clear that while she supports free speech, she wants there to be a “safe space” for all fans.
Sophie Cunningham Rallies
The anti-trans, pro-Cunningham rallies began during the Fever’s game against the Seattle Storm in Seattle, when some groups planned a rally in support of Cunningham and against transgender women in women’s sports.
“Women Are Real, Known Heretic, and Brandi Kruse are organizing a celebratory pre-game fan rally with local female athletes outside Climate Pledge Arena on Tuesday, July 28, before the Indiana Fever take on the Seattle Storm. The rally will show public support for Fever guard Sophie Cunningham, who has faced a wave of criticism since a July 22 ESPN profile in which she expressed support for female-only sports and locker rooms. Cunningham describes her position as one of honesty and care, saying her concern is for young girls who should not have to compete against males. ‘With love is truth,’ she said, and we agree,” the rally’s announcement read at the time.
Since then, a number of other rallies have followed, both in Indianapolis and outside of opposing arenas.
Breanna Stewart Speaks Out
With more rallies planned outside of Saturday’s game between the Fever and the New York Liberty outside of their home stadium in Brooklyn, Liberty star Breanna Stewart spoke out as she made it clear that she wants a safe and inclusive space.
“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” Stewart told a small group of reporters Saturday morning via ESPN. “I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space.”
Stewart said that fans come to games in part because “they can feel like they can be themselves in whatever capacity that is and we don’t want to lose sight of that.”
That said, the Liberty star made it clear that she believes everyone is entitled to their own opinions, and if free speech isn’t allowed, then that would be a much bigger issue.
“If we don’t allow [free speech], we need to like really kind of go back and look at more things. I think the bigger thing is people are trying to divide us as teams, but also as teammates or as opponents,” she said. “This league is incredibly inclusive and what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So, we don’t want to take that platform away.”
